evidence: Plaut. Merc. 374: Ōtium nōn est: mandātīs rēbus praevortī volō.
Plaut. Mil. 252: occupātast, operae nōn est, nōn potest
terms.comment: What Plautus’s people say when they have no time; operae nōn est says the same.
Literally “I have no leisure”. Not found in Lewis & Short or the loci collections in this form; Traupman is the only evidence.

terms.gloss: the day runs out on me: I’ve run out of time
evidence: Cic. Fin. 2.62: sed diēs mē dēficiet
Cic. ND 3.81: Diēs dēficiat, sī velim ēnumerāre …
terms.comment: Cicero’s and Livy’s way of saying that the day would not be long enough for something; in the perfect, diēs nōs dēfēcit, we have run out of time.

phrases.latin: Ōtium nōn est: mandātīs rēbus praevortī volō.
phrases.english: I haven’t time: I want to see to my errands first.
but the day would run out on me

phrases.latin: nec satis temporis ad dēmōnstrandum habēret
phrases.english: and he did not have time enough to show

phrases.latin: Diēs nōs dēfēcit; reliqua crās faciēmus.
phrases.english: We’ve run out of time; we’ll do the rest tomorrow.

sources: Lewis & Short: otium · Lewis & Short: deficio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 89, 109.
